data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Miliaria** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is miliaria?**
- Eruption caused by obstruction of eccrine sweat ducts with leakage of sweat into the epidermis/dermis — common in hot humid climates, neonates (immature ducts), febrile patients, occlusive clothing/dressings, bedridden patients

**Q2. Classify miliaria by the level of duct obstruction.**
- Miliaria crystallina (sudamina): obstruction in stratum corneum — tiny clear superficial dew-drop vesicles without inflammation, rupture easily; neonates, fever
- Miliaria rubra (prickly heat): intra-epidermal (spinous layer) — itchy/prickly red papules and papulovesicles on trunk, flexures, neck; commonest
- Miliaria pustulosa: miliaria rubra with sterile/superficial pustules
- Miliaria profunda: dermo-epidermal junction — non-itchy skin-coloured firm papules after repeated episodes in tropics; associated with anhidrosis and heat exhaustion ('tropical anhidrotic asthenia')

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Excess sweating + occlusion → maceration of stratum corneum → keratin plugs and PAS-positive material (extracellular polysaccharide from Staphylococcus epidermidis biofilm) block the duct → sweat leaks out → inflammation

**Q4. Discuss the composition of sweat (PYQ).**
- Eccrine sweat is hypotonic: water (~99%), sodium chloride (Na 10–90 mmol/L — reabsorbed in the duct), potassium, urea, lactate, ammonia, bicarbonate, amino acids, antimicrobial peptides (dermcidin, cathelicidin), immunoglobulin A; pH 4–6.8
- Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L in cystic fibrosis (diagnostic sweat test)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Neonates: erythema toxicum neonatorum, transient neonatal pustular melanosis, neonatal acne/cephalic pustulosis, candidiasis, herpes, staph folliculitis, impetigo
- Adults: folliculitis, Pityrosporum folliculitis, Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis — sweat-induced), insect bites, varicella (crystallina), drug eruption (AGEP)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Cool environment, air conditioning, fans, loose cotton clothing, reduce sweating and occlusion, frequent cool baths
- Calamine lotion, mild topical steroids for rubra, anhydrous lanolin (prevents duct blockage in profunda), menthol/camphor lotions; antiseptics/antibiotics for pustulosa
- Avoid heavy creams/ointments; treat fever

**Q7. Discuss the composition of sweat (PYQ).**
- Eccrine sweat: 99% water, NaCl (hypotonic — Na 40–60 mmol/l), potassium, urea, lactate, bicarbonate, ammonia, immunoglobulins (IgA), antimicrobial peptides (dermcidin), cytokines; pH 4–6.8
- Apocrine: proteins, lipids, steroids, ammonia, carbohydrates — odourless until bacterial breakdown (thioalcohols, 3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid)

**Q8. What is tropical anhidrotic asthenia?**
- Widespread miliaria profunda in hot climates leading to anhidrosis of trunk with compensatory facial sweating, heat intolerance, weakness, risk of heat stroke; occurs in soldiers/ workers in tropics; move to cool environment, treat miliaria

**Q9. Drug-induced miliaria.**
- Bethanechol, isotretinoin, doxorubicin, clonidine; occlusive dressings/ topical agents; also post-febrile and in patients confined to bed

**Q10. Miliaria in neonates — differentials.**
- Erythema toxicum neonatorum (eosinophils, day 2–3), transient neonatal pustular melanosis (pigmented collarettes, at birth), neonatal acne, neonatal candidiasis, staphylococcal pustulosis, herpes simplex — Gram stain/ Tzanck smear help

**Q11. What is periporitis staphylogenes?**
- Secondary staphylococcal infection of miliaria (pustulosa) forming multiple sweat-gland abscesses in infants (scalp, face, neck, buttocks) — needs systemic antibiotics and cooling

**Q12. Treatment details.**
- Cooling, light cotton clothes, air-conditioning, tepid baths; calamine lotion, mild topical steroid for inflamed rubra; anhydrous lanolin (profunda — unplugs ducts), antiseptics for pustulosa; avoid heavy occlusive emollients; vitamin C supplementation (anecdotal)

**Q13. Describe the clinical types in detail.**
- Miliaria crystallina (sudamina): obstruction in stratum corneum — tiny clear superficial dew-drop vesicles without inflammation; neonates in the first week, febrile patients; rupture easily
- Miliaria rubra (prickly heat): obstruction in mid-epidermis (spinous layer) — itchy/prickly red papules and papulovesicles (non-follicular) on trunk, flexures, covered areas; miliaria pustulosa when pustular
- Miliaria profunda: obstruction at dermo-epidermal junction — skin-coloured papules, no itch, after repeated miliaria rubra in tropics; anhidrosis → heat exhaustion (tropical anhidrotic asthenia)

**Q14. Histopathology.**
- Crystallina: subcorneal/intracorneal vesicle; rubra: spongiotic vesicle in the epidermis around the sweat duct (acrosyringium) with PAS-positive plug and periductal infiltrate; profunda: dermal oedema and lymphocytes around the duct in upper dermis

**Q15. Prevention in neonates and adults.**
- Avoid overheating and over-swaddling; light cotton clothes, air-conditioning/fans, cool baths, avoid occlusive creams (heavy emollients), anhydrous lanolin to clear plugs (profunda)

## Quick spotter facts
- Dew-drop vesicles in febrile neonate — miliaria crystallina
- Prickly red papules in summer — miliaria rubra

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of eccrine sweat glands). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
